body_markdown:
**New figures reveal a significant shift in drug-related fatalities, with cocaine becoming the substance most frequently linked to poisoning deaths for the first time since records began.**


Drug-related deaths in England and Wales remain a serious public health concern, with new official figures revealing a significant change in the substances most commonly involved in fatalities. For the first time since records began in 1993, cocaine has overtaken heroin and morphine as the substance most frequently mentioned in drug-poisoning deaths.


According to figures published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), 5,519 drug-poisoning deaths were registered in England and Wales during 2025. Although this represents a small decrease from the 5,565 deaths recorded in 2024, the overall number remains alarmingly high.


The latest statistics highlight growing concerns about cocaine use, its increasing availability and the potentially fatal consequences associated with its consumption.


## Cocaine Becomes the Leading Substance in Drug-Related Deaths


The ONS reported 1,233 deaths involving cocaine in 2025, equivalent to 20.7 deaths per million people.


This figure placed cocaine ahead of heroin and morphine, which were involved in 1,210 registered deaths during the same year.


The development represents a notable change in the UK's drug-related mortality figures. Historically, heroin and morphine have been among the substances most frequently associated with drug-poisoning deaths.


Although cocaine-related fatalities declined from 1,279 in 2024, the ONS stressed that deaths involving the substance remain historically high. The number is also more than eight times higher than the figure recorded in 2010.


These statistics suggest that cocaine continues to present a substantial public health challenge, despite the modest reduction in recorded deaths during the latest reporting period.


## Overall Drug Death Rate Falls for the First Time Since 2012


One of the more encouraging findings in the latest report is the first annual decrease in the overall drug-poisoning mortality rate in more than a decade.


In 2025, the rate stood at 92.4 deaths per million people, compared with a higher rate in 2024. This marks the first recorded annual reduction since 2012.


However, public health organisations have warned against interpreting this decline as evidence that the wider drug crisis has been resolved.


With 5,519 deaths registered in a single year, the figures demonstrate the continuing scale of the problem. The rise in cocaine-related fatalities also highlights how patterns of substance use and associated risks can change over time.


Continued investment in prevention, treatment and recovery services remains essential to reducing avoidable deaths.


## Why Is Cocaine Use Becoming a Greater Concern?


Charities working with people experiencing drug and alcohol problems have raised concerns about the increasing availability and social acceptance of cocaine.


WithYou, a charity providing support to people affected by substance misuse, has reported that cocaine is becoming more prevalent across many parts of the country.


Robin Pollard, the organisation's head of policy, highlighted changes in the price and accessibility of the substance.


According to Pollard, a gram of cocaine that might previously have cost around £100 before 2020 is now more commonly available for approximately £60 or less. He also noted that smaller quantities have become easier to purchase.


These developments may contribute to wider accessibility, potentially exposing more people to the risks associated with cocaine consumption.


Another concern is the perception that cocaine is a relatively low-risk recreational drug. Its association with nightlife and social occasions can sometimes lead people to underestimate its potential consequences.


However, cocaine use can cause serious cardiovascular complications, including heart attacks and dangerous heart rhythm disturbances. It can also contribute to strokes, seizures and other medical emergencies.


Repeated use may lead to dependence, psychological difficulties and wider problems affecting relationships, employment and personal wellbeing.


## Drug Supply and Increasing Potency Add to the Risks


Mike Trace, chief executive of the social justice charity Forward Trust, said the increase in cocaine-related deaths was not unexpected.


He pointed to record levels of cocaine production in South America, alongside falling prices and concerns about increasing purity.


The relationship between drug production, supply and potency is an important part of understanding the risks facing consumers.


When substances become cheaper and more widely available, accessibility can increase. Higher purity can also create additional dangers, particularly when individuals do not know the strength or composition of what they are taking.


Illicit drugs are not subject to the same quality controls as regulated medicines. Consequently, users may be unaware of the actual contents, strength or potential contaminants in a substance.


This uncertainty makes consumption particularly dangerous and complicates efforts to prevent drug-related harm.


## Men Account for Almost Three-Quarters of Drug Deaths


The latest ONS figures also reveal a substantial difference between male and female drug-poisoning deaths.


Men accounted for 72.5% of registered fatalities in 2025, with 2,622 deaths recorded. Women accounted for 27.5%, representing 993 deaths.


The difference between the sexes has reached a record high, according to David Mais, head of mortality statistics at the ONS.


The average age at death remained relatively consistent with the previous year. For men, the average was 45.5 years, while women had an average age of 48.5 years.


These figures highlight the importance of understanding which groups are most affected by drug-related harm.


Prevention strategies and treatment programmes must consider the different circumstances and support requirements of individuals, including the factors that may influence substance use and access to healthcare.


## Understanding the Limitations of the Latest Statistics


Although the 2025 figures provide important insight into drug-related mortality, the ONS has highlighted an important consideration when interpreting the data.


The published statistics are based on death registrations rather than exclusively on the dates when deaths occurred.


This means that the figures include some fatalities that happened in previous years but were registered during 2025.


The average registration delay was 209 days in England and 253 days in Wales.


As a result, changes in annual registration figures do not necessarily reflect an immediate change in the number of people dying from drug poisoning during that particular calendar year.


This distinction is important when assessing trends and developing effective public health policies.


## The Importance of Prevention, Treatment and Support


The latest findings underline the need for a coordinated response to drug-related harm across England and Wales.


While the reduction in the overall death rate is a positive development, the continued high number of fatalities and the changing pattern of substances involved remain serious concerns.


Improving awareness of cocaine-related risks, expanding access to treatment and providing early intervention could all play an important role in preventing avoidable deaths.


Support should also be accessible to people experiencing dependence, as well as families and communities affected by substance misuse.


Organisations such as WithYou and Forward Trust provide services aimed at helping individuals access support and work towards recovery.


Ultimately, the latest statistics are a reminder that drug-related deaths are not simply numbers. Each fatality represents a person, a family and a wider community affected by the consequences of substance misuse.


Although the first reduction in the overall death rate since 2012 offers some encouragement, the fact that cocaine has overtaken heroin and morphine demonstrates that the challenges surrounding illicit drug use continue to evolve.


Greater awareness, effective prevention and accessible treatment services will remain essential in addressing this ongoing public health issue.
